summary: Farmers in drought-hit regions such as Romania's Bărăgan Plain are being told to change their crop rotations, but a new rotation takes years to prove on real land, and a wrong guess costs a whole season. In 2024 Romania reported about 2 million hectares of crops affected by drought. BioShift is a free web app, with no sign-up, that lets a farmer test a rotation change on the past before risking the future. The farmer picks a field on a map, enters the soil, the terrain and the crops grown each year, and chooses what matters most. BioShift replays every day of weather recorded from 2000 to 2025 through a daily soil-water balance for the current rotation and up to three alternatives, and counts how many seasons each would have hit a water shortage or a heatwave while the crop flowered. On the demo field, sunflower flowered in a heatwave in 17 of 26 summers; chickpea in its place, in 8. Every option shows why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, what we don't know, and what to check with a local agronomist. The weather record is NASA POWER daily data, with NASA satellite layers (MODIS, SMAP, GPM IMERG) on the map.
details:
BioShift helps a farmer answer one question: "If I change my crop rotation, would it have held up better on my field over the last 26 years?" A rotation is the order of crops a farmer grows on the same land, year after year (for example wheat, then maize, then sunflower).

What the farmer sees and does:

  1. Start. The landing page shows a real worked example: a farm near Slobozia, Romania, growing wheat, maize and sunflower, and what changing one crop would have done there. One button starts the analysis. No account, no installation.
  2. Your field. The farmer finds their farm by typing a village name, using their phone's location, tapping the map, or picking one of three example fields (Bărăgan Plain in Romania, Kansas in the USA, Wimmera in Australia). They can draw the field outline to get the hectares. They choose soil type (sandy, loamy, clay), terrain (flat, gentle, steep) and irrigation (none, sometimes, full). Optional NASA satellite layers show vegetation greenness, root-zone soil moisture and the latest rainfall on the map.
  3. Your crops. The farmer builds the current rotation with crop cards, one per year, up to five years, from ten crops: winter wheat, winter barley, winter rapeseed, maize, sunflower, grain sorghum, soybean, field pea, chickpea and alfalfa. They say whether they sow cover crops between harvests. If a chosen crop rarely suited this field in the replay, the app shows a warning with the counted reason (on the demo field, soybean: "too hot and too dry at flowering in 21 of 26 summers"); the crop stays selectable.
  4. Your priorities. The farmer picks up to two goals: more profit, steadier income in bad years, less work and machinery, healthier soil, or using less water. They untick crops they cannot grow or sell, and say whether they have livestock or a hay buyer (otherwise alfalfa is left out).
  5. Results. The current rotation is compared with up to three alternatives, one per size of change: add cover crops, swap one crop, or add a year. A table shows, for each option, the number of bad seasons out of 26 (heatwave or water shortage at flowering), an estimated farm profit in a normal year and a bad year, the number of years with a loss, and the extra work. Each option card has the challenge's five headings: why this option, the evidence (the worst seasons with the rainfall and temperature NASA recorded), the benefits, what we don't know, and what to check with an agronomist. Each carries a confidence badge (Low or Medium) with the reason.
  6. Stress test. Buttons replay the same 26 years 1.5 °C warmer, or 1.5 °C warmer with 20 % less rain, or a custom mix (−30 % to +30 % rain, 0 to +3 °C). The app says whether the best option changes. It is labelled as a stress test, not a forecast.
  7. Make the numbers yours. Profit uses example prices and costs until the farmer types their own. Optional answers (usual sowing months, a soil test, machinery owned, pests seen) each raise the confidence of only the part they inform.
  8. Your plan. For the chosen option: the farm split into equal blocks, a season-by-season timeline per block, and questions for the agronomist. It can be printed, saved as PDF or sent on WhatsApp.
  9. Your field's weather history. A "climate ribbon": one square per month since 2000, coloured by water shortage, extreme heat, heavy rain or frost, with the rotation's crop calendar on top so bad months and flowering months line up. Tapping a square shows that month's numbers. Three trend tiles say whether, for example, hot days are rising, and only call it a trend when a statistical test agrees. A chart compares monthly rain with crop water demand.
  10. Take it to your agronomist. A one-page report for the chosen option, with the farmer's notes, to print or send.
  11. How it works. The method in plain language, the full methodology with sources, and a searchable glossary.

Every results screen says: the tool supports, it does not replace, the farmer's judgment or a local agronomist.

How does it work?

Data in. For the chosen point, the browser requests 26 years (2000-01-01 to 2025-12-31) of daily NASA POWER data: maximum and minimum temperature, rainfall, solar radiation, wind speed and dew point. The demo field's record is saved inside the app (data/demo_field.json, 9,497 days), so the demo works even if the API is slow. Any other point is fetched live; missing values (POWER's −999 fill value) are skipped, and only complete years are used.

Processing. All logic is in plain JavaScript functions in src/model/:

  1. Crop water demand. Daily reference evapotranspiration (how much water a well-watered field loses) by the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation, from POWER temperature, radiation, wind and dew point. Days with missing radiation, wind or humidity fall back to the Hargreaves equation. A unit test checks the result against the FAO-56 worked example.
  2. Rotation calendar. Each crop is placed on a month calendar from its sowing and harvest months, with its FAO-56 crop coefficient curve. Gaps between crops are bare soil or cover crop.
  3. Daily soil-water balance (the replay). For every day of the record: rain in, runoff out on heavy-rain days (USDA curve-number method), crop water use out, limited by how much water the root zone holds (from soil type and rooting depth, FAO-56 tables). Every phase of the rotation is replayed over the whole record, so each crop meets each year.
  4. Counting trouble. A season is "short of water at flowering" when, on at least half its flowering days, dry soil would have let the crop draw less than half the water it needed (FAO-56 water stress coefficient Ks below 0.5). It has a "heatwave at flowering" when 5 or more flowering days exceed the crop's heat limit. Frost in the month after sowing is counted for frost-sensitive crops.
  5. Five scores (0 to 100) per rotation: water, heat, frost, erosion (heavy-rain days of 10 mm or more falling on bare soil, weighted by slope) and nitrogen (share of legume years). Alternatives are found by scoring every single-crop swap and every one-year insertion from the crops the farmer allows; calendar-impossible sequences and ones that bring a crop back sooner than now are dropped.
  6. Money estimate. Yield in each replayed season follows the FAO-33 yield-response equation (yield lost in proportion to water the crop lacked over the whole season), with Ky values from FAO Paper 66. Profit = yield × price − five cost lines. Starting prices and costs are example values for a rain-fed farm in South-East Romania, chosen by us and labelled "Example values, change them to yours".
  7. Ranking. The farmer's goals only change the order of the options; they never change a number.
  8. Trends. Mann-Kendall test with Sen's slope on one value per year. On the demo field, days at 35 °C or more rise by about 6.3 per decade, but p = 0.08, so the app says "weak evidence", not "trend".
  9. Confidence badge. Low when a crop's water parameter is an assumption, when the field is outside 35° to 60° latitude, or when a crop has fewer than 15 replayed seasons; Medium when all water parameters come from FAO-56 tables. High is not reachable yet, and the app says why.

What the demo field shows (Bărăgan Plain, 44.56° N, 27.36° E, loam, gentle slope, rain-fed, wheat → maize → sunflower): 514 mm of rain a year against 1,124 mm of reference evapotranspiration; maize short of water at flowering in 15 of 26 seasons, sunflower in 18 of 26, winter wheat in 10 of 25; sunflower flowered in a heatwave in 17 of 26 summers, chickpea in 8. The same code on a field near Ames, Iowa (42.0° N, 93.6° W) finds maize short of water at flowering in 1 of 26 seasons.

What benefits does it have?

  • A farmer tests a change before betting a season on it, in their own terms ("bad seasons out of 26"), on their own field, with weather that actually happened.
  • Every number can be traced. Each count opens to the worst seasons with the recorded rainfall and temperature. Crop parameters without a published source are labelled as assumptions on screen.
  • It is honest about uncertainty. Confidence badges with written rules, trends only claimed when a test agrees, and a limitations panel on the results page.
  • The agronomist stays in charge. The output is a one-page report with open questions, not an instruction.
  • Free and light. No login, no install, no backend, no cost to run; it works on a phone. The farmer's own numbers stay in their browser only.
  • Works anywhere POWER has data, between 60° S and 70° N, with lower confidence outside the latitudes its crop calendars were written for.

What do I hope to achieve?

  • Short term: show the printed report to agronomists and farmers in Ialomița County (Bărăgan Plain) before spring 2027 sowing decisions, and collect which parts they trust and which they don't.
  • Replace assumptions with local data: sowing months, flowering months and heat limits for local varieties, so confidence can rise from Low to Medium.
  • Add a second rainfall source (for example GPM IMERG monthly totals) to cross-check POWER rainfall; this is the rule for reaching High confidence.
  • A multi-language version, so farmers around the world can use it regardless of the languages they speak.
  • Who could use it: farmers deciding a rotation change, agronomists and extension services who advise them, and farm cooperatives comparing options across fields.

Tools, languages, libraries, frameworks, hosting

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules). No framework, no build step, no backend.
  • Map: Leaflet 1.9.4, loaded from cdnjs with subresource integrity.
  • Charts and icons: hand-written SVG; no chart library.
  • Tests: Node.js built-in test runner, 25 tests (all passing on 15 Nov), including the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith worked example and seasons that must and must not show water stress.
  • Data scripts: a Node.js script (scripts/fetch_demo.mjs) that saves the demo field's NASA POWER record.
  • Fonts: Inter and Manrope from Google Fonts.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages (static files). Source on GitHub: https://github.com/alexvoina2010-prog/field-shift
  • Development: Git, Python's built-in web server for local testing, and Claude Code (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant; see the AI-use section.

Limitations

The weather comes from a NASA grid cell about 50 km wide, built from a weather model blended with observations, so frost pockets, hollows and local storms are averaged away, and it can run hotter or drier than a station on the farm. The replay is rain-fed: irrigation water is not modelled, so for irrigated fields the water count is shown but left out of the total. Sowing months, flowering months and heat limits are generic values for temperate Europe, not local varieties, which is why the top demo option carries a Low confidence badge. Profit uses example prices and costs until the farmer enters their own, counts only water-shortage yield losses (not heat, pests or hail), and leaves out subsidies, rent and the cover crop's seed cost. Pest pressure, soil tests and seed rules are not modelled; they appear as questions for the agronomist. The past is not a forecast: the stress test shows sensitivity, not the future climate.
